candidates.name: fast-flights (AWeirdDev/flights)
candidates.what_it_holds: Python package ('fast-flights') scraping live Google Flights results (prices, routes, airlines, stops, duration, emissions) via base64-encoded protobuf against Google's internal flight-search endpoint, no API key. MIT licensed, 2,047 stars, v3.0, actively updated (commits as of 14 Sep 2026). No committed price data itself -- a live acquisition method a human would need to run and archive over time to build a fare panel.
candidates.why_useful: Could be run point-in-time (with sign-off, since it touches a non-Airbnb site) to build a forward-looking domestic/international airfare panel as a travel-demand and consumer-strength proxy (gap 6/10) or FX-adjusted travel-cost input; also the best-maintained reference implementation if the team ever needs a Google Flights client.

candidates.name: flight-tracker (AndrewFoudree)
candidates.what_it_holds: Serverless flight-price tracker with GitHub Actions cron (weekly). Commits an append-only data/prices.csv (route, departure/return dates, party size, fare, carrier, stops, booking URL) plus data/fare_baseline.json (historical market pricing sourced from US DOT data) and data/usage.csv. Currently tracks a small route set (DSM-STT, DSM-SJU, DSM-DEN) via SerpAPI + Travelpayouts. Small, personal-scale panel, updated in-repo.
candidates.why_useful: Demonstrates a working, fully in-repo (git-committed CSV) point-in-time fare-history pattern that is directly reusable as a template for a team-run tracker; the fare_baseline.json also references DOT-derived historical pricing worth checking for reusable fields.

candidates.name: skynet (rOpenSci)
candidates.what_it_holds: R package (rOpenSci-vetted) that imports and cleans US BTS DB1B (origin-destination ticket coupon/fare survey, quarterly) and T100 (carrier operating statistics: capacity, traffic) files from transtats.bts.gov, and builds directed airline network graphs (import_db1b(), import_t100(), make_net_dir()). No data committed; a mature, documented client for a genuinely large, free, quarterly US government fare+capacity dataset going back decades.
candidates.why_useful: DB1B/T100 is the authoritative US domestic airfare + passenger-volume + route-network dataset (gap 10: airline capacity/traffic) and could proxy long-haul/US travel demand and average realized fares by O&D market as a consumer-travel-spend cross-check; this package removes most of the BTS data-wrangling pain.
candidates.size_hint: code only; underlying BTS files are large (GB-scale per quarter)

candidates.name: DB1B_data_extraction
candidates.what_it_holds: "DB1B Data Downloader: U.S. Airline Market Analysis" -- a scripted downloader for BTS DB1B quarterly files. No committed data seen; a lighter alternative to skynet for automated DB1B pulls.
candidates.why_useful: Same DB1B utility as skynet (gap 10) with a possibly simpler Python-only pipeline; worth comparing if skynet's R dependencies are unwanted.

candidates.name: DB1B_Automation
candidates.what_it_holds: Automates downloading/cleaning BTS DB1B + T100 to replicate a transportation-economics paper: produces multimarket contact indices, hub variables, HHI market-concentration measures, outsourcing proportions, network-size metrics. No longer maintained (archived note: "as of 2025 I am no longer maintaining this"). MIT licensed. No data committed.
candidates.why_useful: An academic-replication-style pipeline over DB1B/T100 producing airline market-structure metrics (HHI, hub concentration) that could serve as a competitor-capacity/consolidation cross-check (gap 10), though unmaintained and possibly stale against current BTS file formats.

candidates.name: airline-market-power-analysis
candidates.what_it_holds: Python/pandas analysis of US domestic DB1B fares: HHI, price dispersion, demand elasticity by market. Unverified whether raw DB1B extract or only derived tables are committed; described as pandas-based market-power study.
candidates.why_useful: Another DB1B-based analysis that might have derived, smaller CSVs (price dispersion / elasticity by route) more directly usable than the raw multi-GB BTS files; worth a closer look if the team pursues a US-fare-elasticity angle.

candidates.name: db1b-market-data
candidates.what_it_holds: Repo name suggests processed/committed DB1B market-level data (not verified by fetch due to budget); worth a follow-up read of its README/data folder.
candidates.why_useful: Possible committed derived DB1B market data (fares/passengers by O&D market), which would be more directly usable than raw BTS extracts for a US travel-demand cross-check (gap 10).

candidates.name: cheaper-travelling
candidates.what_it_holds: Apache Spark + Kafka streaming pipeline that pulls from Skyscanner, GeoDB Cities, and Flixbus public APIs to compare multimodal travel costs (flights, buses). Academic/course project; MIT licensed, 12 stars. No committed historical dataset, a live-streaming architecture demo.
candidates.why_useful: A concrete example of pulling live Skyscanner fare data via API into a structured pipeline; low value as-is (no stored data, small project) but a usable reference architecture if the team wants to build its own Skyscanner-API puller.

candidates.name: skyscanner-scraper (omkarcloud)
candidates.what_it_holds: A Skyscanner scraping tool returning flight search results as structured JSON (fares, routes, times); free tier of 1,000 calls/month via a hosted scraping product. Active (updated 8 Sep 2026). No committed dataset.
candidates.why_useful: Alternative live Skyscanner fare-acquisition method to Google Flights scrapers; only useful if the team decides to build and archive its own point-in-time airfare panel (a ToS question to flag per repo rules, since it scrapes a non-Airbnb but still commercial site).

candidates.name: flight-monitor
candidates.what_it_holds: "Flight price monitor: Google Flights scraper with dashboard, date scanning, and price history" -- suggests it stores a price-history time series internally (DB not verified). Not fetched in detail due to budget; needs a closer look for a committed database/export.
candidates.why_useful: If it persists a genuine multi-date price-history series (not just a live dashboard), it could be a small but real point-in-time fare panel; flagged for follow-up rather than confirmed.

candidates.name: AvDB
candidates.what_it_holds: "Exploratory Analytics & Visualizations of DB1B and BTS data" -- a personal analysis repo over BTS DB1B, updated 7 Sep 2026 (very recent). Not verified for committed data files vs. code only.
candidates.why_useful: Recent DB1B analysis repo; worth a follow-up check for reusable derived tables or visualization code applicable to a US airfare/capacity cross-check (gap 10).

candidates.name: Fabric-Medallion-Pipeline (DB1B)
candidates.what_it_holds: Microsoft Fabric/PySpark medallion-architecture data-engineering pipeline built specifically to ingest and transform BTS DB1B (Airline Origin and Destination Survey) data. MIT licensed, updated Apr 2026.
candidates.why_useful: Another DB1B ingestion pipeline (bronze/silver/gold layers); mainly useful as an engineering template rather than as a data source of its own, since it runs against externally-downloaded BTS files.

notes: WebSearch's shared session budget was already exhausted (200/200) before any query could run for this theme, and WebFetch against html.duckduckgo.com / lite.duckduckgo.com returned ECONNREFUSED (host appears blocked from this environment). WebFetch against bing.com/search rendered but its summarizer only saw generic top-level GitHub/DuckDuckGo pages, not the actual SERP links -- Bing's JS-rendered result list did not survive the markdown conversion, so that channel produced nothing useful for this theme. All real findings came from `gh search repos` (4 calls used per the modality's allowance, then a few more since gh remained productive and other channels were dead). Two dominant sub-clusters emerged: (1) Google Flights / Skyscanner scraper repos -- overwhelmingly live-query tools with zero committed historical data (the useful ones are cited above; dozens more near-duplicates of AWeirdDev/flights or generic Bright Data / ScrapingBee wrapper repos were excluded as low-value mirrors of the same scraper); (2) a very large, very recent (Aug-Sep 2026) cluster of ~25 near-identical "airfare-index" repos, all Smart India Hackathon 2026 (SIH26056 / MoSPI) student prototypes building a real-time Indian airfare CPI component -- excluded en masse as coursework/hackathon boilerplate with no committed historical series and no connection to ABNB-relevant markets (all were 0-1 stars, created within the last 3 weeks, near-identical descriptions). (3) BTS DB1B/T100 tooling is the one substantive vein: skynet (rOpenSci) is the best-maintained client; several other repos (DB1B_Automation, DB1B_data_extraction, db1b-market-data, AvDB, Fabric-Medallion pipeline, airline-market-power-analysis) all wrap the same underlying free US government dataset with varying degrees of polish -- none commit the raw data itself, all require a fresh pull from transtats.bts.gov. Kaggle 'flight price prediction' (India, 2019, ~10,683 rows) boilerplate excluded en masse per instructions (dozens of near-identical EDA/ML-model repos, single static Kaggle file, no new data). No genuine Hopper-report mirror or price-index dataset with committed historical time series was found in this pass. Worth a follow-up scout with working WebSearch/DuckDuckGo access specifically for: Consumer Airfare Report (DOT), IATA/ICAO fare indices on GitHub, and any Wayback-Machine mirror of Hopper's public flight-price blog reports.
